note: Placed at Doboka in the Kopili–Jamuna valley. Its extent is not recorded; the shape is the present Hojai and West Karbi Anglong districts.
Early Kamarupa: the Brahmaputra valley around Pragjyotishpura. No boundary is recorded for the 4th–5th centuries; the Karatoya is the traditional western limit.
Davaka is absorbed and Bhutivarman's grant (6th c.) reaches the Sylhet region, so the kingdom stretches from the Karatoya to the Bharali and south into the Surma valley.
Bhaskaravarman at his height: ally of Harsha, host of Xuanzang (c. 640).

label: Gauda (campaign reach)
note: The undated Nidhanpur charter names a victory camp at Karnasuvarna. This approximate campaign overlay is separate from the adopted Paundravardhana / Ratnapitha region; its date, extent and duration are uncertain.
Same core as the Varman kingdom, without firm evidence of the Sylhet grants. Capital at Haruppeswara (Tezpur) under the later kings.
Harjaravarman (c. 815–832) and Vanamalavarmadeva rule to the Dikrong on the north bank; Harjara's Tezpur rock inscription (829) is the best dated record.
Ratnapala and Indrapala issue grants across the valley. The south bank of the Brahmaputra is the core.
The Paschimbhag plate of Srichandra (c. 930) grants land in Srihatta. Later local kings (the Gaur line) are known mainly from tradition.

Schematic successor-region context. Authority is unevenly attested through Vaidyadeva, Vallabhadeva’s genealogy, the unnamed defenders of 1206, Visvasundara, Samudrapala (1232) and Sandhya. This is not one unified state or a measured frontier.

label: Western Kamarupa
note: Approximate western intervention zone for Bengal’s Palas and the Tingyadeva–Vaidyadeva sequence. The 1110–1139 interval and Manas cutoff are display assumptions, not securely attested conquest dates or frontiers.
The Kolong in Nagaon becomes the western limit after the Dimasa capital Dimapur is sacked (1536).

Treaty of Majuli display, 1563–1580: north-bank Ahom territory lies east of the Subansiri, sharing the actual mapped river trace with the Koch eastern boundary. The south-bank interpretation is retained separately. The later 1581 Bharali frontier is a distinct phase.
Inherited north-bank Bharali and south-bank Kolong context, before the 1614–1616 frontier transition. Exact earlier recovery dates remain qualified.

label: Mir Jumla's occupation
note: Mir Jumla occupies Garhgaon (March 1662 – January 1663); the Ahom king withdraws to the hills.
Kings are now made and unmade by Burmese armies (1817, 1819).

Dimapur on the Dhansiri; the Dikhow is the frontier with the Ahoms (Ahom account). Both Karbi Anglong districts and Dima Hasao are included in the adopted hill-domain reconstruction. User-adopted maximum-extent envelope also includes all three Barak Valley districts. Their simultaneous possession throughout this display interval is not independently verified; modern districts are geographic proxies, not medieval frontiers. Revision: no retreat is inferred from the 1523 Chutia annexation. The 1526 and 1531 Dhansiri campaigns appear as contested reach; the settled-border transition uses the existing approximate 1532 stage.

Approximate 1532–1536 Dhansiri-frontier stage following the 1526 and renewed 1531 campaigns. 1532 is an annual display convention, not the first Ahom–Kachari clash. The 1523 Chutia conquest does not trigger this retreat. Other adopted hill/Barak holdings persist; Dimapur is sacked in 1536.
Capital at Maibong. Yasho Narayan (1583–1601) is the strongest king; Rudra Singha's Ahom army takes Maibong in 1706.

label: Dimasa · hill–Barak extent
note: User-adopted hill–Barak reconstruction: all of modern Dima Hasao, Karbi Anglong, West Karbi Anglong and the three Barak Valley districts (Cachar, Hailakandi, Karimganj), with Hojai. Shown in the Khaspur phase from the existing 1745 merger anchor. Modern districts are geographic proxies; this combined envelope is not independently verified as simultaneous possession. Parts of Karimganj have competing Sylhet histories.

label: Tularam's hill state
note: After the British annex the Cachar plains (1832), Tularam Senapati keeps the North Cachar hills until 1854.

label: Sylhet
note: Shah Jalal and the Sultanate's army take Sylhet (1303).
Husain Shah's Kamata, held up to Hajo by 1502.

User-adopted eastern-Meghalaya display, using the former Jaintia Hills district as a modern geographic proxy, clipped to Meghalaya and explicitly excluding Assam. It does not depict the kingdom’s historical Jaintiapur/Sylhet plains or imply that modern district boundaries were medieval frontiers.

Koch Hajo core between Sankosh and the atlas’s qualified Barnadi reference, explicitly clipped to present-day Assam. Eastern Darrang influence is shown separately as reach. The 1612 invasion and 1613 annexation follow in stages; earlier cross-border campaigning is not merged into this core.
Founded by Kamal Narayan, Chilarai's brother, as governor of the Cachar plains.

label: Sylhet
note: Sylhet under Mughal Bengal (and from 1717 the Nawabs of Bengal).

Annexed western Kamrup: separate north-bank Barnadi reference and south-bank Kajali-post envelope. Ahom tributary Darrang and temporary raids are distinct; the south-bank straight post cutoff is schematic.
The Treaty of Asurar Ali (1639).
Kamrup and Darrang ceded by the Treaty of Ghilajharighat.
After the 1667 Ahom recovery, Mughal settled possession is west of Manas. Saraighat in 1671 fails to reverse that recovery.
Guwahati returns to Mughal possession in 1679. Barnadi-side and Kajali-post rearward envelopes are approximate display conventions; an exact all-locality frontier for 1679–1681 is not established.
Goalpara (the land between the Sankosh and the Manas) under Mughal Bengal.

label: Matak · autonomous
note: 1805 settlement: autonomous Matak government under the Barsenapati. River-bounded reconstruction between the Brahmaputra and Buri Dihing, ending at the Sadiya meridian. Modern river traces and the eastern cutoff are approximate; not today’s Tinsukia district. The government survives the Burmese troubles; 1826 and 1835 Company agreements do not make it part of Purandar’s restoration.
Burmese occupation of the whole valley; Chandrakanta Singha is driven out (1821–1822).
The British take Guwahati (March 1824) and advance up the valley.

label: East India Company
note: The Company receives the Diwani of Bengal (1765), including Goalpara and Sylhet.
The First Anglo-Burmese War: British troops occupy Lower Assam.
British occupation after the 1824–1825 campaigns. Yandabo (24 February 1826) records Ava’s renunciation of claims/interference; Matak and Sadiya retain separate local arrangements.
The Cachar plains are annexed (1832) after the death of Govindachandra.

label: Purandar Singha's Upper Assam
note: 1833 restoration as a protected ruler paying tribute: north-bank eastern context from Biswanath and south-bank context east of the Dhansiri. Matak and Sadiya remain separate. Bank envelopes are reconstructed and approximate. The annual map shows the post-annexation position in 1838.

British-administered valley/plains context, with separate Matak, Sadiya and Purandar layers cut out while active. Purandar’s territory passes to direct administration in 1838; Matak direct management follows in 1839. Modern Assam district contours remain approximate proxies.
Remaining Tularam hill territory is annexed in 1854. Modern Assam and Sylhet reference contours approximate the regional extent. Garo, Khasi and Naga developments are shown as separate dated layers.

label: Province of Assam
note: Assam Chief Commissionership from 1874. Separate layers show Jaintia, Garo, Khasi relationships and the growing Naga Hills district; no whole-modern-Nagaland annexation is implied.

label: Province of Assam
note: The northern and southern Lushai administrations merge under Assam on 1 April 1898. The separate Lushai layer starts before this administrative transfer.

label: Eastern Bengal and Assam
note: Eastern Bengal and Assam from 16 October 1905. Dacca, Chittagong and Rajshahi divisions except Darjeeling, plus Malda, join Assam. This uses modern district proxies; it is not a surveyed 1905 boundary or the whole present country of Bangladesh.

label: Province of Assam
note: Assam returns to separate administration in 1912. Other regional layers continue independently.

label: Province of Assam
note: Separate Assam administration. The North-East Frontier Tracts appear as a context overlay, not a claim that all modern Arunachal was fully administered in 1914.

label: Assam
note: Indian Assam province/state context. Naga district reference is approximate. NEFA/frontier administration is shown separately; Manipur and Tripura retain their distinct sequences. Sylhet division is only a modern proxy for the transferred region.

label: Assam
note: Assam’s constitutional extent includes NHTA through 1962, with its special administrative relationship shown as a dotted overlay. Nagaland formally separates in 1963. Modern reference contours approximate the regional extent.

label: Assam
note: Meghalaya, Mizoram and Arunachal are separated (21 January 1972); the capital moves from Shillong to Dispur.

label: East Pakistan
note: Country context using the present Bangladesh outline as an approximate reference. Sylhet is not shown as a separate modern territory; Karimganj remains in India.

label: Bangladesh
note: Country context using the present Bangladesh outline as an approximate reference. Sylhet is not shown as a separate modern territory; Karimganj remains in India.

label: NHTA · special unit within Assam
note: Administrative unit within the State of Assam from 1 December 1957 under section 2 of the 1957 Act. Separate central administration does not mean full constitutional separation. Nagaland statehood and formal separation follow on 1 December 1963.

label: Meghalaya
note: Full statehood from 21 January 1972, following autonomous-state status within Assam since 1970.

label: Mizoram · Union Territory
note: Union Territory from 21 January 1972. Statehood follows on 20 February 1987.

label: Arunachal · Union Territory
note: Separate Union Territory from 21 January 1972; NEFA territories cease to form part of Assam under section 7 of the 1971 Act. Statehood follows on 20 February 1987.

Approximate stage of western advance through the Dhansiri campaigns, ending with the 1536 sack of Dimapur. 1532 is a playback anchor, not a surveyed boundary date.

label: Chutia centre ≈

label: Chutia centre ≈

label: Chutia evidence ≈
note: Sadiya, Habung-region evidence from 1392 and Ghilamara evidence from 1401; the 1428 charter adds a named Habung authority. Symbolic localities do not establish a continuous frontier or conquest date.

Southern river frontier follows the same mapped Dehing vertices as the early Ahom northern boundary; the north-bank domain is a separate Brahmaputra-bounded sector.
Western political focus after Sandhya’s reorganisation; an inherited successor region, not a new conquest from zero. Bounds schematic.

label: Eastern authority uncertain

Schematic western core during rival 14th-century rulers. Approximate chronological division, not a dated contraction.

label: Contested reach

Late-14th/early-15th-century western Kamata focus. Arimatta traditions do not justify an empire to Sadiya; separate Bhuyan seats lie east.
Early Khen western base around Kamatapur; c.1440 conventional foundation, bounds schematic.
Intermediate consolidation-stage reconstruction around Chakradhwaj’s approximate reign. No district-specific annexation date is implied.
Nilambar’s wider late-15th-century domain. c.1480 is a conventional reign-stage anchor. Kamatapur falls to Husain Shah in 1498.

Mid-15th-century reconstructed plains domain, following the earlier Sadiya and western grants and the 1442 Tamreswari inscription. This is an approximate domain context, not a claim of conquest in 1442 or continuous control of every intervening village. Upland Arunachal is not automatically included. Southern river frontier follows the same mapped Dehing vertices as the early Ahom northern boundary; the north-bank domain is a separate Brahmaputra-bounded sector.

label: Chikna foothill base
note: Small Chikna-region founding envelope, not the later Karatoya–Barnadi kingdom. 1515 is the conventional dynastic start; early kingship and campaign dates differ. The Saralbhanga-side location is regional; other edges are schematic.

label: Koch local consolidation
note: Illustrative lower-Assam expansion from the foothill base toward the Sankosh–Manas plains. 1520 is a display anchor within the poorly dated Bhuyan campaigns, not a documented conquest of this complete outline.

label: Koch western consolidation
note: Western Kamata and Duars enlargement toward the Karatoya, retaining the founding area. c.1527 is one research account’s kingship/consolidation anchor; the timing of each capital move and this intermediate frontier is uncertain.

Later Biswa Singha domain context, approaching the Karatoya–Barnadi envelope. 1533 follows the Turbak campaign aftermath and Ahom contact; this mature extent is reconstructed, not evidence of every district being conquered in that year.
Naranarayan inherits the consolidated western kingdom. His accession does not automatically annex the later eastern campaigning zone.
Western core during the first major Ahom war. The separate hatched north-bank zone is campaign reach and the Narayanpur advance, not permanent annexation.
After the 1547 Pichala defeat the eastern campaigning layer is removed. The western core remains; diplomatic and military preparation precedes the 1562 advance.
Renewed eastern campaign under Chilarai. Eastern hatching records wartime reach; tributary rulers retain their own kingdoms.

Post-Majuli settlement display, 1563–1580: on the north bank the Subansiri is the shared Koch–Ahom frontier. Koch holds west of the river; Ahom holds east. The south-bank line retains the separate approximate Kolong interpretation. Majuli camp and Garhgaon occupation markers record campaign presence, not permanent island or whole-kingdom annexation. This treaty frontier ends before the 1581 successor-state phase.

label: Koch campaign reach
note: 1546–1547 north-bank campaign toward Narayanpur; removed after Pichala. The broad corridor is schematic campaign reach, not complete annexation.

label: Koch campaign reach
note: 1562–1563 eastern invasion toward Garhgaon, shown schematically in the 1562 annual frame. Hatching marks campaign reach, not settled administration.

label: Bhuyan Confedaracy
note: Surviving western chiefdom context during gradual Koch consolidation. The 1533 removal is a display anchor, not the exact defeat date of every chief. River-sector extents remain approximate.

label: Bhuyan Confedaracy

label: Dhansiri campaigns ≈
note: Contested Ahom–Kachari corridor for the 1526 campaign and renewed 1531 fighting at Marangi. Hatching records campaign pressure, not a dated survey of continuous Ahom administration. Earlier Kachari core remains beneath this reach layer until the approximate 1532 transition.

label: Eastern dependencies ≈
note: Approximate Darrang-side influence in the older Koch reconstruction. This is not the same as the better-attested Sankosh–Barnadi core; local and Ahom authority varied. Clipped to Assam.

label: Koch Hajo · under invasion
note: Last independent annual frame during the 1612–1613 invasion. The western campaign overlay shows Mughal advance; exact month-by-month conquered parcels are not known.

label: Western invasion ≈
note: Schematic first-stage invasion through the Dhubri/western sector during the 1612–1613 campaign. Hatching is military reach, not an assertion that every parcel changed hands in 1612.

label: Kamrup resistance ≈
note: Post-annexation resistance and Mughal reconsolidation, 1614–1615. Hatching qualifies the annexed core; it does not resurrect a single independent Koch Hajo kingdom.

label: Eastern invasion · repulsed
note: Attempted eastward advance in 1615–1616. The campaign layer disappears after the Ahom reversal; it is not permanent Mughal annexation of Darrang.

label: Western Bengal · 1576
note: Rajmahal ends the Karrani sultanate, but the eastern delta is not yet subdued. This low-confidence western envelope is a regional reconstruction, not proof of uniform occupation of every modern district.

label: Western Bengal · contested
note: Mughal authority faces rebellion and Afghan/local resistance. The western footprint remains a context envelope, with hatching to mark contested authority; exact annual district boundaries are unresolved.

label: Western Bengal
note: Western consolidation precedes the decisive eastern campaigns. Bhati, Sylhet and the Chittagong coast are not automatically annexed in 1576.

label: Western base · advance east
note: Islam Khan begins the decisive eastern campaign. Dhaka becomes the provincial base in 1610; the separate eastern hatching records advance rather than instant delta-wide possession.

label: Bhati and delta submissions
note: Musa Khan and the Bhati chiefs submit; Jessore, Bakla and Bhulua are brought under control. Sylhet’s remaining Afghan resistance is kept separate until the next stage.

label: Bengal · coast not yet annexed
note: Eastern Bengal and Sylhet are consolidated by 1612. Chittagong remains outside Mughal control; the three Chittagong Hill Tracts districts and the northern West Bengal hill/princely districts are excluded from this direct-rule proxy.

label: Bengal · Chittagong added
note: Chittagong is conquered in 1666. The coastal district proxy is added; this does not turn every modern hill/princely region of West Bengal and Bangladesh into directly annexed Mughal land.

label: Bengal nawabs · nominal Mughal rule
note: Bengal’s nawabs govern with increasing autonomy under nominal Mughal sovereignty. The Company receives the Diwani in 1765; this is not continued direct administration from Delhi.

label: Contested western authority
note: Regional rebellion context, not a surveyed set of rebel estates.

label: Eastern campaign ≈
note: The eastern campaign is represented schematically before the 1611 submissions; hatching does not count as core territory.

label: Eastern chiefs & Afghan resistance
note: Mixed independent and semi-independent chiefs, including the Bhati confederacy and Afghan authorities. This is a regional context, not a single state or a list of precisely mapped estates.

label: Sylhet · Afghan resistance
note: The remaining Sylhet Afghan authorities are distinguished from the Bhati submissions; the next annual stage shows 1612 consolidation.

label: Afghan Bengal ≈
note: Late Afghan/Karrani Bengal context before Rajmahal. Modern district proxies do not imply identical historical borders or uniform direct authority.

label: Bengal · Company/British rule
note: Lowland Bengal context after the 1765 Diwani transfer. This geographic proxy excludes northern hill/princely regions rather than retroactively annexing them on the Diwani date.
Inherited bank-specific core during the Koch Hajo collapse. Political/military reach toward Barnadi is separate hatching; it is not automatic annexation of all Kamrup.

After Samdhara, tributary Darrang carries Ahom political reach to Barnadi on the north bank. Direct core remains separately distinguished. Kajali is a south-bank frontier-post reference, not a surveyed meridian boundary. Pandu/Hajo and later western operations are temporary reach layers.
Late-1630s reversal: conservative eastern core with contested western space. The Bharali/Kolong rearward envelope is a schematic annual war-stage convention, not a documented 1638 cadastral frontier.

Treaty of Asurar Ali: Barnadi on the north bank and Asurar Ali on the south. Includes the Ahom political sphere east of the agreed line, including dependent chiefs. The atlas uses its inherited qualified Puthimari/Bornadi river reference.

Guwahati and Lower Assam are taken during the 1658–1660 expansion window. 1658 is the adopted annual anchor; other accounts date Guwahati to 1659 and wider Kamrup to 1660. Manas is the conservative settled envelope; farther-west reach to Sankosh is separate hatching.

Mir Jumla occupies Guwahati in February and Garhgaon in March 1662. The rearward Ahom bank envelope distinguishes the lost Kamrup territory from the farther-east occupation overlay; it is not a claim that the invasion stopped at these rivers.
Ghilajharighat aftermath: Bharali-side retreat on the north bank and Kolong-side retreat on the south. The 1667 recovery is shown in 1667 itself, not delayed until 1668.
Lachit recovers Guwahati and Pandu in 1667 and pushes the Mughal forces back toward Manas. Saraighat in 1671 defends the recovered position; it is not the first capture of Guwahati.
Guwahati is surrendered in 1679. This post-based rearward envelope separates the two banks; the exact frontier outside the documented forts is unresolved and remains low confidence.
Gadadhar Singha’s final recovery of Guwahati in 1682 establishes the lasting Manas frontier. Both banks use the same river reference. Later episodes must not be confused with the 1667 recovery.

label: Barnadi-side reach ≈
note: Koch Hajo collapse and Ahom involvement create political/military reach toward Barnadi. Not a claim that Darrang was already directly annexed in 1614.

label: Darrang · Ahom tributary
note: Balinarayan/Dharmanarayan is installed as tributary ruler of Darrang after the 1615–1616 fighting. This layer represents dependent political reach to Barnadi, distinct from directly administered Ahom core.

label: Pandu/Hajo advance ≈
note: Gait dates the November 1617 advance and capture/fortification of Pandu, followed by a failed Hajo assault and retreat. This is temporary military reach in the modern Guwahati vicinity, not continuous annexation of the whole city or Kamrup.

label: Western campaign ≈
note: The 1636–1637 western campaign captures Hajo and other garrisons and wins local submissions. The wide envelope is temporary campaign/tributary reach, not a durable annexation of every intervening locality.

label: Farther-west reach ≈
note: Sources describe the Koch forces driven beyond Sankosh in the 1658–1660 expansion. Farther-west possession is not assumed to be permanent or uniformly administered.

label: Kamrup war-stage ≈
note: Conservative war-stage occupation envelope following the late-1630s Ahom reverses. The treaty phase that follows has different north- and south-bank terms.

label: Occupied Kamrup
note: Mir Jumla’s occupation removes Kamrup/Guwahati from Ahom control in 1662; farther eastern invasion is a separate occupation overlay.

label: Sadiya · local authority
note: Locality symbol only. Khamti local jurisdiction coexists with British political officers and a garrison. Intervention reduces that jurisdiction before the 1839 rising; the annual display does not assert an unchanged constitution throughout this interval.

label: Khasi states
note: Modern Khasi-region districts locate several separate local states. This is regional context, not their individual borders or evidence for a unified kingdom. The 1829–1833 war is shown by its dated event marker.

label: Khasi states · British relations
note: Local states remain distinct from British station lands. Agreements and British paramountcy must not be read as blanket direct annexation. Modern Khasi-region contours are a contextual proxy.

label: Jaintia · British from 1835
note: 1835 annexation. This retains the adopted hills-only Jaintia proxy and does not claim to reconstruct the kingdom’s Jaintiapur plains.

label: Garo Hills · district 1869
note: District at Tura in 1869; the whole interior is not yet administered. The modern Garo-region outline provides context only. The 1872–1873 campaign follows.

label: Garo Hills · British from 1873
note: Extension of administration after the 1872–1873 campaign. Modern Garo districts provide an approximate regional footprint, not surveyed 1873 boundaries.

label: Naga Hills · district 1866
note: Regional context for the documented district/expansion stage, assembled from modern district reference polygons. Exact colonial boundaries are unresolved; the shape does not annex the whole of modern Nagaland. Stages: district 1866, Lotha country 1875, Ao country 1889.

label: Naga Hills · Lotha stage
note: Regional context for the documented district/expansion stage, assembled from modern district reference polygons. Exact colonial boundaries are unresolved; the shape does not annex the whole of modern Nagaland. Stages: district 1866, Lotha country 1875, Ao country 1889.

label: Naga Hills · Ao stage
note: Regional context for the documented district/expansion stage, assembled from modern district reference polygons. Exact colonial boundaries are unresolved; the shape does not annex the whole of modern Nagaland. Stages: district 1866, Lotha country 1875, Ao country 1889.

label: Lushai Hills · occupation stages
note: Regional context for posts and campaigns from 1889–1890, followed by separate northern/southern administrations. The modern Mizoram outline does not imply effective control of every village in 1889.

label: Lushai Hills · annexation 1895
note: Formal proclamation dated 6 September 1895, published 7 September, according to Mizoram Land Revenue Department. Modern state outline approximates the region; northern/southern administrations merge under Assam in 1898.

label: Lushai Hills · Assam from 1898
note: Unified Lushai Hills district under Assam from 1 April 1898. This is an administrative merger, distinct from the earlier occupation and 1895 proclamation. Modern outline is approximate.

label: Frontier tracts · context
note: North-East Frontier Tracts / 1914 boundary context. Modern Arunachal outline is for regional orientation only; it does not establish uniform British occupation, administration or an uncontested boundary. Local powers and effective administration varied.

label: Manipur kingdom ≈
note: Early-19th-century regional context; modern border proxy.

label: Manipur · restored kingdom ≈
note: Gambhir Singh recovers Manipur with British support in 1825. The next annual stage distinguishes the British protection/political relationship from direct annexation.

label: Manipur · British paramountcy
note: British forces take over on 27 April 1891; the subsequent princely settlement places Manipur under British paramountcy. British-coloured hatching shows that relationship while retaining local identity. It is not an ordinary district of Assam.

label: Manipur · acceded to India
note: Instrument of Accession signed 11 August 1947. Orange hatching shows accession to the Dominion of India while internal government continues; the transfer to central administration follows on 15 October 1949. This is distinct from membership of Assam.

label: Manipur · India, central administration
note: Merger agreement transfers administration to the Dominion of India on 15 October 1949. Solid Indian colour shows central administration. Part C constitutional status starts on 26 January 1950; this is not annexation into Assam.

label: Manipur · India, Union Territory
note: Union Territory from 1956; statehood from 21 January 1972.

label: Manipur · India, state
note: Statehood from 21 January 1972.

label: Manipur · Burmese occupation
note: 1819–1825 occupation/recovery sequence; annual map uses 1825 for Gambhir Singh’s recovery. Modern Manipur outline is a regional proxy, not the wartime frontier.

label: Tripura kingdom ≈
note: Early-19th-century kingdom context. NCERT dates the protectorate stage to 1809; earlier British intervention and lowland estates are distinct. The modern outline is a proxy.

label: Tripura · acceded to India
note: Instrument of Accession signed 13 August 1947. Orange hatching shows accession to the Dominion of India while internal government continues; the transfer to central administration follows on 15 October 1949. This is distinct from membership of Assam.

label: Tripura · India, central administration
note: Merger agreement transfers administration to the Dominion of India on 15 October 1949. Solid Indian colour shows central administration. Part C constitutional status starts on 26 January 1950; this is not annexation into Assam.

label: Tripura · India, Union Territory
note: Union Territory from 1956; full statehood from 21 January 1972.

label: Tripura · India, state
note: Statehood from 21 January 1972; separate from territories reorganised out of Assam.

label: Nagaland
note: Statehood from 1 December 1963, following the Naga Hills–Tuensang Area.

label: Meghalaya · autonomous within Assam
note: Autonomous state within Assam from 2 April 1970. Context overlay preserves Assam beneath it. The modern outline is approximate for 1970; the Shillong exceptions are not reconstructed. Full statehood follows in 1972.

label: Mizoram
note: Statehood from 20 February 1987; formerly a Union Territory.

label: Frontier administration / NEFA
note: NEFA/frontier areas remain constitutionally included in Assam with special central/frontier administration. Section 7 of the 1971 Act ends that inclusion when Arunachal Pradesh becomes a separate Union Territory on 21 January 1972. Modern outline is a regional reference.

label: Arunachal Pradesh
note: Statehood from 20 February 1987; formerly a Union Territory.

label: Manipur · British protection
note: Restored local kingship with British protection and political relations, distinguished from the stronger post-1891 settlement. Yandabo contains a recognition provision, not a transfer of Manipur to an Assam district. The regional outline is approximate.

label: Tripura · British protectorate
note: NCERT dates British protectorate status to 1809. Local Manikya government continues; the hatching identifies British protection without equating Hill Tippera with a directly administered Assam district. Modern outline is a regional proxy.

label: Tripura · British paramountcy
note: A British Political Agent is appointed in 1871. Tripura remains a princely state under British paramountcy; British-coloured hatching makes the imperial relationship visible. Political supervision associated with Eastern Bengal and Assam from 1905 does not turn Hill Tippera into an ordinary Assam district.

label: Manipur · India, Part C state
note: Part C state of the Republic of India from 26 January 1950; central administration had begun on 15 October 1949. Union Territory status follows in 1956.

label: Tripura · India, Part C state
note: Part C state of the Republic of India from 26 January 1950; central administration had begun on 15 October 1949. Union Territory status follows in 1956.

label: Assam
note: Nagaland is a separate state from 1 December 1963. Meghalaya becomes autonomous within Assam in 1970; full separation follows in 1972. Mizoram remains part of Assam until its 1972 Union Territory transition.

label: Sikkim · separate kingdom
note: Postwar kingdom context, not part of Assam. Modern regional outline is a proxy; no claim is made that statehood began in 1947.

label: Sikkim · Indian protectorate
note: Protectorate treaty signed 5 December 1950; Sikkim remains a separate kingdom rather than a full Indian state. Modern regional outline is a proxy.

label: Sikkim · India, state
note: Indian statehood from the officially observed date of 16 May 1975. Not carved out of Assam.
